Many tissues are organised along a depth axis: cortical layers, the epidermis,
the airway wall from epithelium to submucosa. Spatial transcriptomics can place
every spot or cell on that axis, but most tools analyse one section at a time.
This guide shows how to compare depth patterns **across donors and disease
groups** with LongOmicsTraj, treating ordered depth windows the way the package
treats visits in a longitudinal study:

| Longitudinal study | Spatial study |
|---|---|
| visit | depth window (e.g. upper, deep, white matter) |
| subject | tissue section |
| group or arm | donor, or disease group |

The workflow has five steps, each one function call:

1. **Pick a reliable depth map** with `lot_consensus_restart()`.
2. **Build depth-window pseudobulk** with `lot_spatial_pseudobulk()`.
3. **Check that depth patterns replicate across donors** with `lot_topology_agreement()`.
4. **Label every gene's depth pattern** with the standard LongOmicsTraj workflow, using `center = "relative"`.
5. **Find genes whose depth pattern differs between groups** with `lot_query()`.

## What you need

* A **count matrix** (genes × spots or cells), from Visium, Xenium, CosMx, MERFISH or similar.
* A **depth coordinate or layer label for every spot**. Any method works: GASTON
  isodepth, Belayer, distance from a tissue boundary, or annotated layers.
  If your depth model has random restarts, keep all of them for step 1.
* **Several sections per donor** if possible, and **at least three donors or
  groups**. Relative centring (step 4) needs three or more groups.

## Example data

We simulate six donors (three healthy, three with disease), two sections each,
and 150 genes. The simulation builds in the three problems we met in real
cortex data:

* most genes fall from the deep window into white matter **in every donor**
  (shared biology that must be kept);
* donor H2 has a burst of mitochondrial reads in its upper window, which after
  library-size normalisation makes every other gene appear to rise from upper
  to deep (a **donor-specific technical offset** that must be removed);
* 20 genes rise into white matter **only in disease** (the signal we want).

```{r simulate}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(LongOmicsTraj))
set.seed(42)
donors <- c("H1", "H2", "H3", "D1", "D2", "D3")
G <- 150; genes <- c(paste0("gene", 1:(G - 10)), paste0("MT-", 1:10))
step <- 0.6
up1 <- sample(c(-1, 0, 1), G, TRUE, c(0.15, 0.7, 0.15))             # upper -> deep
up2 <- ifelse(runif(G) < 0.5, -1, sample(c(0, 1), G, TRUE, c(0.8, 0.2)))  # deep -> WM: many fall
up1[(G - 9):G] <- 0; up2[(G - 9):G] <- 0                             # MT genes flat
disease_genes <- which(up1 == 0 & up2 == 0)[1:20]                    # flat in health ...
base <- rnorm(G, 0, 0.8); base[(G - 9):G] <- 1

spots <- list(); counts <- list()
for (d in donors) for (s in 1:2) {
  xy <- expand.grid(x = 1:20, y = 1:20)
  depth <- (xy$y - 1) / 19 + 0.05 * sin(xy$x / 3)                    # gently curved layers
  depth <- pmin(pmax(depth, 0), 1)
  w <- cut(depth, c(-Inf, 1/3, 2/3, Inf), labels = FALSE)
  eff2 <- up2
  if (startsWith(d, "D")) eff2[disease_genes] <- 1                    # ... rise into WM in disease
  logmu <- base + step * (outer(rep(1, G), w >= 2) * up1 + outer(rep(1, G), w >= 3) * eff2)
  if (d == "H2") logmu[(G - 9):G, w == 1] <- logmu[(G - 9):G, w == 1] + 3.5   # MT burst
  id <- paste0(d, "_s", s, "_", seq_len(nrow(xy)))
  counts[[length(counts) + 1]] <- matrix(rpois(G * nrow(xy), 3 * exp(logmu)), G,
                                         dimnames = list(genes, id))
  spots[[length(spots) + 1]] <- data.frame(section = paste0(d, "_s", s), donor = d,
                                           condition = ifelse(startsWith(d, "H"), "Healthy", "Disease"),
                                           true_depth = depth, row.names = id)
}
counts <- do.call(cbind, counts); spots <- do.call(rbind, spots)
dim(counts)
```

## Step 1: pick a reliable depth map

Depth models such as GASTON are trained from several random restarts. The
default is to keep the restart with the lowest training loss, but in the human
cortex this produced a folded or misoriented depth map in half of the sections.
`lot_consensus_restart()` instead keeps the restart that agrees best with all
the others. It needs no labels.

Here each section gets ten restarts: seven faithful, two folded around the
middle of the tissue and one with its direction flipped. In real use, the
columns are the depth coordinates your tool returned for each restart.

```{r restarts}
pick <- lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(spots)), spots$section), function(i) {
  t <- spots$true_depth[i]
  restarts <- cbind(sapply(1:7, function(r) t + rnorm(length(t), 0, 0.04)),
                    folded_1 = abs(t - 0.5), folded_2 = abs(t - 0.45),
                    flipped = 1 - t + rnorm(length(t), 0, 0.04))
  res <- lot_consensus_restart(restarts)
  depth <- restarts[, res$best]
  if (stats::cor(depth, t, method = "spearman") < 0) depth <- 1 - depth   # orient (see note)
  data.frame(spot = rownames(spots)[i], depth = depth, chosen = res$best)
})
pick <- do.call(rbind, pick)
table(chosen_restart = pick$chosen)
spots$depth <- pick$depth[match(rownames(spots), pick$spot)]
```

No section chose a folded restart. Agreement is measured with absolute
correlations, so a flipped restart can be chosen; orient the chosen depth with
one known marker or landmark (for example a myelin gene increasing towards white
matter). Here we orient against the simulated truth for brevity.

## Step 2: build depth-window pseudobulk

Cut the depth coordinate into ordered windows and average each section's
spots within each window. Use `window_col` instead of `depth_col` if you
already have layer labels.

```{r pseudobulk}
pb <- lot_spatial_pseudobulk(counts, spots, section_col = "section", group_col = "donor",
                             depth_col = "depth", breaks = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1),
                             window_levels = c("upper", "deep", "WM"))
head(pb$metadata)
```

`pb$expression` and `pb$metadata` go straight into `lot_create()`.

## Step 3: check that depth patterns replicate across donors

Before interpreting anything, check that depth patterns are reproducible. For
the healthy donors, `lot_topology_agreement()` labels every gene's depth
pattern in each donor and reports the fraction of genes with the same pattern
in all of them. The p-value comes from re-running everything after shuffling
window order within each section.

```{r agreement}
healthy <- pb$metadata$group %in% c("H1", "H2", "H3")
E_h <- pb$expression[, healthy]; M_h <- pb$metadata[healthy, ]
visits <- c("upper", "deep", "WM")
agree <- lapply(c(none = "none", median = "median", relative = "relative"), function(cc)
  lot_topology_agreement(E_h, M_h, visits, center = cc, nperm = 19))
data.frame(agreement = sapply(agree, `[[`, "agreement"),
           kappa = sapply(agree, `[[`, "kappa"),
           null_mean = sapply(agree, function(a) mean(a$null)),
           p = sapply(agree, `[[`, "p"))
```

Without centring, donor H2's offset breaks agreement. Median centring removes
the offset but also removes the real, shared fall into white matter. Relative
centring removes only what is specific to one donor. With 19 permutations the
smallest possible p-value is 0.05; use 999 for a paper.

## Step 4: label every gene's depth pattern

Now run the standard workflow on all six donors, each donor as a group, with
`center = "relative"`.

```{r workflow}
lot <- lot_create(expression = pb$expression, metadata = pb$metadata, assay = "rna",
                  visit_levels = visits, feature_type = "gene")
lot <- lot_from_empirical(lot, assay = "rna", visits = visits, group_col = "group",
                          visit_col = "visit", estimator = "empirical", verbose = FALSE)
lot <- lot_compute_deltas(lot, assay = "rna", visits = visits, center = "relative")
lot <- lot_compute_thresholds(lot, assay = "rna", visits = visits, method = "hybrid",
                              k = 0.25, verbose = FALSE)
lot <- lot_map_to_ots(lot, assay = "rna", visits = visits, verbose = FALSE)
```

Always look at the offsets that were removed. The shared shift is kept; only
H2's upper-to-deep offset is large:

```{r offsets}
off <- as.data.frame(lot@results$visit_centring)
off[order(-abs(off$offset)), ][1:4, ]
```

An offset in one donor only is likely technical. An offset shared by all
donors is likely biology and is kept by relative centring.

## Step 5: find genes whose depth pattern differs between groups

`lot_query()` with `conditions` finds genes that satisfy a topology condition
in every named group. Here: flat in all three healthy donors, rising into
white matter in all three disease donors.

```{r query}
hits <- lot_query(lot, conditions = list(H1 = "flat_flat", H2 = "flat_flat", H3 = "flat_flat",
                                         D1 = "flat_up", D2 = "flat_up", D3 = "flat_up"))
found <- unique(as.data.frame(hits)$object_id)
c(found = length(found), true_positives = sum(found %in% genes[disease_genes]),
  planted = length(disease_genes))
```

Requiring the pattern in every donor is strict, which keeps false positives
low; relax it with `NOT()` or by querying fewer donors if your study is larger
and more heterogeneous.

## Practical recommendations

These come from applying the workflow to human cortex (Visium, 12 sections from
3 donors) and lung fibrosis (Xenium), and from simulations with known truth.

* **Depth.** Keep all restarts of your depth model and choose by agreement, not
  by loss. Orient the chosen depth with one known marker.
* **Windows.** Two to four windows with at least 20 spots each per section work
  well. Name them by depth order, not by expected cell types.
* **Centring.** Use `center = "relative"` with three or more groups. Use
  `"median"` only when you are confident that most genes do not change between
  windows. Always inspect `results$visit_centring`.
* **Thresholds.** The hybrid rule with `k` between 0.25 and 0.5 gave stable
  results. Avoid quantile thresholds for depth data: they label most changes
  as flat by construction.
* **Statistics.** Treat donors, not spots or cells, as the units of
  replication. Use at least 999 permutations for reported p-values, and report
  the excess over the permutation null (`z`) alongside p.
